Admittedly, one might argue that printed newspapers remain necessary since they follow strict journalistic standards and undergo rigorous fact-checking procedures, allowing readers to trust the information they receive. Those on this side of the debate also claim that print remains essential for individuals who lack technological awareness or access, ensuring that they are not excluded from current affairs. However, this line of reasoning fails to consider that many reputable online platforms also have printed versions, suggesting that the accuracy of information is no longer determined by its format. Moreover, digital literacy and access to affordable Internet services and smart devices are increasing across age groups, making the claim that online news is less reliable and harder to access less convincing.

Manipulation is more difficult to tackle, since introducing legislation to check the content of social media posts and adverts can itself become a form of manipulation if authorities control which opinions may be expressed. Decisions about what should be prohibited may be subjective, meaning that any attempt to regulate harmful content must be handled carefully to avoid taking away freedom of speech.

As for manipulation, social media platforms could be required to label sponsored content and work with independent fact-checkers to flag misleading posts, while schools could teach media literacy so that users learn to verify information before sharing it.
